progression.startsWith: Prepare and precipitate an ion sample. The video opens: Here's a strange first step for an analysis. Weigh out half a gram of dried potassium sulfate. You already know how much sulfate is in it, because you know its formula.
progression.stopsAfter: stating the aim and variables of a recovery investigation; calculating the expected precipitate mass from a known sample; carrying out the method in order with quantities (acidify, hot, excess barium, completeness check, digest, pre-weighed paper, rinse, wash until the washings test clear, look at the filtrate, oven, desiccator, constant mass); calculating percentage recovery; judging reliability, accuracy and validity with evidence; writing the risk rows for barium chloride, dilute hydrochloric acid, silver nitrate, hot apparatus and heavy-metal waste.

teaching.task: Why would a chemist weigh out a sample whose sulfate content is already known, and analyse it anyway? How do you carry out a gravimetric sulfate analysis safely, and use recovery to judge whether the method can be trusted?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) a known sample tests the method (1); (2) recovery, the aim and the variables (2); (3) the expected mass from the formula (3); (4) prepare, acidify, heat, add excess Ba²⁺ slowly, check completeness (4); (5) digest or not, the prediction (5); (6) filter, rinse, wash, test the washings, look at the filtrate (6); (7) dry to constant mass and weigh (7); (8) recovery from the means (8); (9) reliable within each set, the gap bigger than the spread; accuracy against the known value; the cloudy filtrate shows the loss; repeats can't recover lost crystals (9); (10) the comparison is valid because only digestion changed, and the method measures only sulfate; the standard must be pure and dry (10); (11) hazards and controls, waste (11); memory aid (12); attempts (13 to 16); decision rule and handoff (17); key notes (18).
teaching.conversationalApproach: the strange first step is weighing out half a gram of dried potassium sulfate whose sulfate content you already know from its formula, so the practical asks why analyse it anyway, how to carry out a gravimetric sulfate analysis safely, and how recovery shows whether the method can be trusted. The aim asks whether digesting the precipitate improves the recovery, the mass of barium sulfate collected as a percentage of the mass you should get, with digestion as the independent variable and recovery as the dependent. The expected mass comes first: moles of potassium sulfate, one sulfate per formula unit and one barium sulfate per sulfate, a target of 0.670 g. The method runs in order with quantities: dissolve, acidify, heat nearly to boiling, add excess barium chloride slowly and check that a drop more gives no new cloudiness. Set A is not digested and set B digests for about thirty minutes, both cool before filtering through a pre-weighed fine paper, and the washings are tested with silver nitrate until they stay clear; set A's filtrate is faintly cloudy and set B's is clear. Each paper dries to constant mass. Set B recovers about 99% and set A about 94%; the trials agree within each set, so the gap is real, and the cloudy filtrate shows set A's systematic loss, which repeats cannot fix. Validity rests on one changed variable, a method that weighs only sulfate and a pure, dry known sample. The risk table contrasts barely soluble barium sulfate with toxic dissolved barium chloride, which the teacher prepares and dispenses, and sends filtrate and washings to heavy-metal waste. The memory aid is recovery equals found over expected times a hundred: under a hundred means something was lost, over means something extra was weighed. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Here's a strange first step for an analysis. Weigh out half a gram of dried potassium sulfate. You already know how much sulfate is in it, because you know its formula. So why analyse it? To test your method. If it recovers all the sulfate you put in, you can trust it on a real sample. If not, you'll see how much it loses.
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "To check a gravimetric method for sulfate, a student dissolved 0.350 g of pure, dry anhydrous sodium sulfate, Na₂SO₄, in water, acidified the solution and added excess barium chloride solution. The barium sulfate precipitate was filtered, washed and dried to constant mass. Its mass was 0.561 g. (a) Calculate the percentage recovery of sulfate. (b) State what this result suggests about the accuracy of the method. M(Na₂SO₄) = 142.04 g mol⁻¹; M(BaSO₄) = 233.39 g mol⁻¹." Answer: 0.350 ÷ 142.04 = 2.46 × 10⁻³ mol; 1 : 1, so expected BaSO₄ = 2.464 × 10⁻³ × 233.39 = 0.5751 g; recovery = 0.561 ÷ 0.5751 × 100 = 97.5% (a guard digit kept; 0.561 ÷ 0.575 would give 97.6%); close to 100% but a little low, so the method loses a small amount of sulfate (slightly low, not exact). Crossed mistake: "0.561 ÷ 0.350 × 100 = 160%" (masses of different substances divided directly). (A2) "Two sets of students tested whether digestion improves the recovery of barium sulfate. Set C digested the precipitate for 30 minutes and washed it with three portions of warm distilled water. Set D did not digest the precipitate and washed it with one portion. Both sets were filtered at room temperature. Set C's mean recovery was higher than Set D's. Explain why this comparison is not valid, and propose a change that fixes the problem." Answer: two variables changed (digestion and washing); less washing can leave dried-on impurities that add mass (raising D's recovery), so the difference can't be put down to digestion alone; fix: wash both sets the same way, until a few drops of the washings stay clear with silver nitrate. Crossed mistake: "repeat each set more times" (reliability, not validity; every repeat still has unequal washing; s07's crossed habit).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "conduct investigations and/or process data involving:; gravimetric analysis; precipitation titrations" This video is the investigation for gravimetric analysis. The method's reasons and the calculation were chem-m8-c02; precipitation titrations were chem-m8-c01 (processed as data; p01 is cut); practice with both is chem-m8-g01. this video prepares students to carry out and evaluate the investigation; it does not claim that watching it is conducting it. It starts by preparing and precipitating a sulfate sample, and stops at filtering, drying, weighing and evaluating recovery. It teaches: why an analyst runs the method on a sample of known composition first (a check standard, pure dried potassium sulfate); percentage recovery (mass collected as a percentage of the mass expected); the aim (does digesting the precipitate improve recovery?) with independent, dependent and controlled variables; the expected mass from the formula; the hands-on quantities and order (dissolve, acidify, heat, add excess barium chloride slowly with stirring, the completeness drop, digest or not, filter through pre-weighed fine paper, rinse, wash with warm water, test the washings with silver nitrate until they stay clear, look at the filtrate, dry, desiccator, weigh to constant mass); reading three trials per set for reliability (spread against gap); judging accuracy against the known value, with the cloudy filtrate as evidence of the cause; validity of the comparison and of the method; the risk table and disposal. Recalled, not re-taught: each method step's reason and the calculation chain (c02), AgCl as a white precipitate (c01, c03b later), validity, reliability, accuracy and word, feature, fix (s07). Not here: ignition in a crucible, co-precipitation mechanisms, the chloride version (g01 practises AgCl data), titration (c01), blank corrections.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m8-c02: sulfate yellow-green; barium pale violet; chloride green; silver pale grey; precipitate white; givens and units navy; the current answer bright; earlier lines dim. The two sets keep fixed colours across chips, lanes, dots and gauges (set A grey-blue, set B teal). Hazards terracotta, controls green. Board layout (three zones, constant, as chem-m7-p05): top-left the short task line; the centre holds the apparatus plate; the right third holds the current card (method step, variables, calculation board, results, validity card, risk table), one at a time. Clutter rule: at most three bright text items; every label dims when its sentence ends. Plates and owner rules: no people or hands (weighing, pouring, stirring, rinsing and moving the watch glass are coded motion; the tongs are a coded outline); apparatus as painted plates listed by filename, never stretched; at most about three bright text items, earlier lines dim; the calculation as a separate task, equation and grouped givens, one stage at a time; "Pause here to answer." then a 10 s countdown with the full worded question kept on screen; no givens card in the attempts, givens underlined in the feedback as they are used; brief feedback (about 15 to 30 s) with one crossed-out mistake; original HSC-style questions only; real GHS classifications, school rules to be checked against NSW Chemical Safety in Schools; Australian spelling; no em dashes; conversational narration; no absolute claims; optional key notes hold. No human figures.
